o: Lord God, as I begin this day, I lift my voice to give You thanks. You are great and worthy of all praise, and Your love reaches the farthest places on earth. Thank You for life, for the health You give me and for the opportunity to serve You today where You have placed me.

I pray that You kindle in me a willing heart. May I not stay closed up in my own affairs, but look with compassion on those around me and remember that Your Word is for all peoples. Give me courage to speak of You with simplicity and gentleness, and give me a heart that loves people as You love them.

Bless the missionaries, the translators of Your Word and all who serve in difficult places. Give them strength, protection and joy. And bless also my home, my work and the people I will speak with today. Guide me by Your Spirit so that each of my actions reflects Your goodness. May this day be an opportunity to declare Your wonders. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 11, 1793, the English missionary William Carey landed in Calcutta, India. He was born in 1761 in a village in England, into a humble family, and had worked as a shoemaker before becoming a Baptist pastor. From his youth, he was interested in learning about the peoples of the world and in learning languages.

Carey was convinced that Christians should carry the Gospel to all nations, an idea that, in his time, was not accepted by everyone. In 1792 he published a work on the obligation of Christians to use means to spread the Gospel to peoples who did not know it. It is recalled that, in a sermon that year, he exhorted with these words: “Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.”

In April 1793, he left England with his family and his companion John Thomas, sent by the Baptist missionary society that had been formed for this purpose. After several months of travel, they arrived in Calcutta in November. The beginnings were not easy: the East India Company viewed missionaries with suspicion, and Carey had to face financial difficulties, illness and an unfamiliar language.

With patience, he devoted himself to learning Bengali and other languages, and in time he settled in Serampore, a Danish colony, with other companions. There, translations of the Bible were printed that ended up being published, in whole or in part, in dozens of languages and dialects. Carey's work, which began with an uncertain voyage, helped awaken the modern missionary movement and reminds us that the command of Jesus remains current.
m.c: Walk today with the certainty that the same God who accompanied his servants in distant lands goes with you in every place. May his grace give you courage for each task and may his promises sustain you when your strength fails. His faithfulness covers you from this moment.
m: Jesus said to his disciples: “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.” This word was not only for a few heroes of history, but for all who follow the Lord. The story of William Carey reminds us that many great works begin with a simple decision: to obey what God has said, even if the road is uncertain.

At first glance, the command to go into all the world might seem distant to us. Perhaps we think our world is home, work, the neighborhood or school. And that is exactly where one begins. The psalmist says it this way: “Sing to the LORD, bless his name; tell of his salvation from day to day.” Notice those words: from day to day. Declaring God does not always mean traveling far; it means living each day in such a way that others see his goodness.

Today you can put this into practice in concrete ways. Greet with affection someone who often goes unnoticed. Offer your help without expecting anything in return. If someone asks how you are, answer with gratitude and not with a complaint. And if a conversation opens up, simply share what God has done in your life. You do not need long speeches; a sincere testimony is enough.

Carey also teaches us perseverance. His beginnings were slow and full of trials, but he kept working, translating and teaching. Do not be discouraged if, today, what you are doing seems small. God uses what is small for great things. Attempt something for him in faith, trust in his help and wait with hope. Declare his glory among the nations, as the psalm says, and leave the result in his hands.

o: Lord and Shepherd of my life, at the end of this day, I come with a grateful heart. Thank You, because You have cared for me at every step, You have given me food, shelter and people who love me. Thank You, because even when I am distracted or wander away, You seek me with patience and bring me back to Your side.

I acknowledge that very often I have strayed without realizing it. I let myself be carried away by rushes, by worries and by things that give me no rest. Forgive me, Lord. Thank You, because You do not leave me lost, but come to meet me with love. Today I rest in the assurance that I am Yours and that You are my shepherd.

I pray for those who feel lost tonight: for those who are far from their family, for those who doubt Your love and for those who carry sorrows. Let them feel Your nearness. Take care of my home and my loved ones while we sleep. May I wake renewed, knowing that Your goodness accompanies me all my days. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Jesus told stories that showed the heart of the Father, and one of the most beloved is that of the lost sheep. He asked those who were listening: “What do you think? If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the mountains and go in search of the one that went astray?”

This was a scene everyone understood. In those days, many people lived by raising livestock and knew well the value of each animal. A shepherd knew how many sheep he had and recognized each one. If one was missing, he did not stay at ease, saying he still had ninety-nine. He went out to look for it, traveled through difficult places and did not stop until he found it.

Jesus went on to say that, if the shepherd finds it, he rejoices over that one more than over the ninety-nine that never went astray. Imagine his joy as he lifts the sheep onto his shoulders and returns home. There is no reproach or punishment in this story, only a shepherd who rejoices at having found what was his.

And then came the lesson: “So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” Every person matters to God. No one is a number, no one is forgotten. Tonight, even if the day has been long or even if you have felt far away, remember that the Shepherd does not lose sight of you. His love seeks you, finds you and carries you in his arms.
t.c: End this day with gratitude, knowing that the Shepherd cares for you even in the dark. Leave the pending tasks and the doubts in his hands, for he watches over you. May you sleep quietly and may his peace guard your heart until dawn.
m: Psalm 100 says: “Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.” It is a very tender declaration. We are the sheep of his pasture, that is, people who live under the care of a Shepherd. This truth is especially comforting when the day ends and we come home tired.

The parable of the lost sheep teaches us that God does not give up on us. Sometimes we think that if we make a mistake, or drift a little away from him, he will not want us near him. But Jesus says the opposite: the Shepherd goes out in search of us. His love does not depend on our perfection. What he desires is to have us back in his company, and the door is always open.

Tonight you can apply this truth with a brief review of your day. Think of the moments when you felt you were drifting from God: a harsh word, a complaining thought, a rush that made you forget prayer. This is not about accusing yourself, but about returning. Simply tell God: “Here I am, Lord.” He is already waiting to welcome you.

Then, give thanks. The psalmist invites us to enter his gates with praise, for the LORD is good and his steadfast love endures forever. Mention in a low voice something you are grateful for: a meal, an unexpected help, a smile. And finally, think of someone who may feel lost. Pray for that person and, if you can, look tomorrow for a way to draw near with affection. In this way we will be a reflection of the Shepherd who never tires of seeking.
